svg.title: Sensor wiring to the Teensy, and how the circuit gets built twice
svg.desc: Top: the two sensor runs — two Hall latches on the drive hub with their pull-ups at the Teensy, and the AS5600 on I2C at the kingpin — showing conductor counts, voltages and the cable treatment each needs. Bottom: the two-stage build, a solderless breadboard on the bench and soldered perfboard on the vehicle, with the rule that separates them and the consumables the BOM never bought.
svg.text: Two sensors, four wires each — and the circuit gets built twice on purpose
Both runs are long, both pass a PWM'd motor, and neither is 5 V. Everything below follows from those three facts.
DRIVE — 2 × DRV5013 Hall latch, at the rear hub
printed bracket
clamps the housing nose
spaced
4 conductors
3.3 V · GND · A · B
AWG 22, ~1 m
Teensy 4.1
A, B → two pins of ONE hardware QDC
3.3 V and GND from the Teensy itself
10 kΩ pull-up on A and on B — HERE
at the receiving end, not at the sensor
The latch output is OPEN DRAIN. Without a pull-up the line never rises.
It does not look like a missing resistor — it looks like a dead sensor, which is the expensive way to
find it. The resistor kit on [#7] carries 10 kΩ; this was confirmed on arrival.
Add 1 nF from each output to GND at the Teensy. Not 100 nF — with 10 kΩ that is a 1 ms corner and a
count at walking pace is only 11 ms. 1 nF gives 10 µs: kills PWM pickup, keeps the edge square.
Cable treatment — all three matter, and none costs anything
■ Twist A with GND and B with GND, or use a 4-core with a drain. The return path is what makes
a long logic run quiet; a loose bundle beside a motor lead is an antenna.
■ Route away from the motor leads — cross them at 90° if they must meet.
■ Ground at the star point only — the sensor GND goes back to the driver's star, not to any
convenient chassis screw. A second ground path is FMEA row 5.
STEERING — AS5600 on I²C, at the kingpin
chassis bracket
faces the magnet cap
on the kingpin bolt
gap set by AGC, not by eye
Ø4 × 1.63 is a small magnet
4 conductors
3.3 V · GND · SDA · SCL
Teensy 4.1
I²C, address fixed at 0x36
one device on the bus — by design
run the bus at 100 kHz, not 400
I²C is the fragile link on this vehicle, and it is worth saying why
It was designed as a board-level bus. This run is ~1 m from a front kingpin to a box in the bay,
past a motor. It will work — but it is the thing that will misbehave first.
■ Twist SDA with GND and SCL with GND. ■ Add 4.7 kΩ pull-ups at the Teensy, in parallel
with whatever the breakout already has — faster edges over cable capacitance.
The escape hatch is already inside the chip: use its PWM output
The AS5600's OUT pin can be configured as PWM instead of analog. One wire, timing-based,
and far more robust over a metre of cable than I²C — a corrupted bit becomes a slightly wrong
angle rather than a hung bus.
Bench it on I²C, keep PWM in reserve. Configuring it is an I²C register write, so prove the bus
works on the desk first — you need it once, to turn it off.
Build it twice — and the rule that separates the two is not "prototype then tidy up"
ON THE BENCH — solderless breadboard, yes
You are right that one is needed, and the build pages never said so —
they only warned against breadboard on the vehicle, which is a different claim.
What it is for
■ Prove the pull-ups and the QDC counts before anything is soldered
■ Find the AS5600 on the bus and tune AGC with the magnet in a vice
■ Try pin assignments freely — they are not fixed yet, and changing a
soldered board costs an evening while changing a breadboard costs nothing
What it must never carry
■ Relay coil current — 600 mA through spring clips
■ The MOSFET gate pulldown — an intermittent contact there floats the
gate, and a floating gate chatters the relays between STOCK and DBW
Bench the SIGNAL side on a breadboard. Bench the AUTHORITY side on
the perfboard you will actually fit — build that one first.
ON THE VEHICLE — soldered perfboard, always
A breadboard contact is a spring clip on a vehicle that vibrates. The
circuit is part of the authority chain, so an intermittent joint is not
a glitch — it is an unplanned mode change while moving.
Three rules for the board that goes in

text.tspan: 1 · The Teensy sits in FEMALE HEADERS, not soldered down.

svg.text: Thirteen students, one bricked bootloader, ₩74,250 a board.

text.tspan: 2 · Every off-board wire lands on a screw terminal.

svg.text: A sensor swaps without a soldering iron, and cable movement pulls on
a terminal rather than on a solder joint — which is how joints crack.

text.tspan: 3 · Pull-ups and the 1 nF live on the board, beside the Teensy.

svg.text: Not on the sensor end, not in the middle of a loom.
Two boards, not one: the signal board on the logic side, and the
relay-driver board in the power box. Same split as the enclosures.
And this is where "every part is bought" turns out to be wrong
§1.2.4 specifies perfboard, screw terminals and a printed enclosure for the relay-driver board. The Order Log never bought any of them —
[#7] carries relays, MOSFETs, resistors and diodes, and stops there. The assembly consumables were specified in one document and
procured in neither. Nothing here is expensive; all of it stops work on the day it is missed.
Still to buy
■ 만능기판 / perfboard — 2 boards per vehicle, 6 + spares
■ Screw terminal blocks, 5 mm pitch — 2 and 3 way, ~8 per vehicle
■ Female headers, 2.54 mm — two 24-way rows per Teensy
■ Solderless breadboard + jumper set — bench only, 1–2 of each
■ Heatshrink assortment — the #8a pigtail splice needs it, and nothing bought any
■ 1 nF ceramics — check the resistor kit's companion; if absent, 20 of them
■ 4.7 kΩ for the I²C pull-ups — confirm the 30-value kit has it
Roughly ₩40–60k for the fleet, against ₩545,464 of headroom.
